content:
(I suspect there's not many people besides me who care about this corner of the library, but I figured I'd ask anyways.)

The ordinal derivative of a normal function Ordinal -> Ordinal (which is entirely unrelated to the usual derivative) is the unique function Ordinal -> Ordinal which enumerates its fixed points. More precisely, the derivative of f is strictly monotonic and its range is exactly the set of fixed points of f. Normality is an indispensable condition, since otherwise there's no way to guarantee that f has a cofinal set of fixed points.

We have a definition docs#Ordinal.deriv for the ordinal derivative in Mathlib. This has no normality requirement, and is instead defined via limit recursion. Most of the file is dedicated to proving that in the case where the function is normal, the derivative does indeed have the properties required of it.

However, using some basic results about club sets (which I have scattered across various open PRs), one can sidestep this entirely. That is, we can write something like enum f.fixedPoints, and directly prove that it satisfies the characterizing property of enumerating the fixed points, instead of tediously going through limit induction. Doing this makes it hard to justify keeping the junk values, in my view.

So basically, my proposal is to require normality in Ordinal.deriv, and prove the characterization in terms of limit recursion after the fact. Any objections?
@Bhavik Mehta @Dexin Zhang

the current definitions of Ordinal.nfpFamily and Ordinal.derivFamily seems like a different construction that just happens to give the derivative in the case of a normal function, it could be generalized to multi-argument functions
What generalization do you have in mind?
derivFamily is weird because it's defined in terms of an indexed family when really what you want is a small set of functions
That one's my fault

Violeta Hernández said:

What generalization do you have in mind?

after thinking about it for a while I discover I can define my "generalization" in terms of derivative

I'm not sure I follow the argument here - what exactly do club sets let you sidestep? What's the reason to drop the junk values? The usual principle is that we don't want to have propositional arguments in definitions, I don't see how club sets are relevant here for that choice.
The current definition is only useful for proving the characterization we actually want, but we can do that more directly, so the current definition isn't useful.
At least that's my view
So are you proposing to delete it? Or change it? What do you want to change it to?
Modulo some potential refactors I want to change the definition to enumOrd f.fixedPoints
docs#Ordinal.enumOrd
I guess doing this doesn't require carrying an IsNormal assumption either, but it would change the junk values to something that behaves worse
But ultimately all of the theorems should require an IsNormal assumption anyways

Sorry, I was really tired earlier, I think I didn't articulate my point very well.

The problem with the current definition of deriv is that it takes a lot of work to prove that it satisfies the correct "enumerator function of fixed points" characterization, even with the normality assumption. I want to redefine it so that this fact is obvious, but doing so would change around the junk values unpredictability. So before doing this, I would like to refactor the API so that we don't depend on the current junk values. i.e. instead of writing theorems for the case where f is a raw function, or monotone, or strictly monotone... we only write theorems for the case where f is normal.
That makes a lot of sense, sounds good to me.
